items.title: Silks, Crowns & Fairies  | Dressing a 17th Century Queen
items.description:
In 1632, Henrietta Maria attended a royal masque dressed as Divine Beauty. Royal masques were hugely popular in the 17th century. They were theatrical and elaborate parties, with singing, dancing and drinking. Queens such as Anne of Denmark and Henrietta Maria would have worn elaborate costumes to have taken part in these performances. In this video, our experts in fashion history demonstrate how these Queens would have got dressed before they embarked on their Royal Masque.

global_silver_linings.title: Organizations Rally to Reunite Lost Pets with Owners Following Earthquake in Japan
global_silver_linings.snippet: An inspiring story of solidarity between pet owners comes from Japan, recently rattled by a magnitude 7.1 earthquake. In the wake of the disaster that destroyed homes and claimed over 3 dozen lives, an organization that acts as a digital hub for lost pet notices has amplified the signal of these notices, and worked to […] The post Organizations Rally to Reunite Lost Pets with Owners Following Earthquake in Japan appeared first on Good News Network .
global_silver_linings.reason: In the aftermath of disaster, volunteers and rescue organizations came together to help families find their beloved pets — a reminder that compassion extends to every member of a household, even in the hardest moments. These efforts bring real comfort to people who have already lost so much.

global_silver_linings.title: Young high school teacher’s response to getting hit on by students sets a brilliant example
global_silver_linings.snippet: "You have to set your boundary, loudly, in front of everybody." The post Young high school teacher’s response to getting hit on by students sets a brilliant example appeared first on Upworthy .
global_silver_linings.reason: A young teacher's clear, confident boundaries in a difficult situation shows students what healthy self-respect looks like in action — and that's a lesson that will stick far longer than any textbook. Good mentorship often happens in exactly these unscripted moments.

global_silver_linings.title: Podcast Transcript July 31st, 2026— Liquid air batteries, dolphins saved by plastic bottles, and an empty weekend a month
global_silver_linings.snippet: Episode Description: Dolphins fatally swim into fishing nets because the nylon is acoustically too similar to water for their echolocation to pick up. A researcher at Newcastle University wondered if attaching something that does produce an echo might change that. The dolphin-saving solution may surprise you.
global_silver_linings.reason: From dolphins rescued using repurposed plastic bottles to liquid air batteries pointing toward cleaner energy storage, this roundup is a quiet reminder that human ingenuity keeps finding ways to work with — and for — the natural world. Even a simple idea like a monthly empty weekend suggests we're rethinking what a sustainable, balanced life can look like.

discovery_articles.title: Kawran Bazar in Dhaka, Bangladesh
discovery_articles.snippet: Kawran Bazar is a massive wholesale market located in the center of Dhaka, and one of the largest wholesale markets in South Asia by some accounts. While it technically operates 24/7, some of the liveliest times are in the middle of the night and wee hours of the morning. 2 am fruit auction, anyone?
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Somewhere in Dhaka right now, while you sleep, merchants are auctioning mangoes and jackfruit under fluorescent lights at 2 a.m. — a city within a city that runs on a schedule the sun never sees.

discovery_articles.title: Burpee Covered Bridge in Gaspereau Forks, New Brunswick
discovery_articles.snippet: Back when public displays of affection were more taboo, covered bridges popped up in every corner of the province of New Brunswick. Built mostly in the late 1800s and early 1900s, the wooden, roofed structures helped farmers and travelers get safely from one side of a river to the other, even in the snowy, harsh winters of yesteryear. But in their heyday, “covered bridges” wasn’t the only term people used to identify the river-crossing spans.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: New Brunswick's covered bridges weren't just engineering — locals called them 'kissing bridges,' because the brief, sheltered darkness gave courting couples their only socially tolerated moment of privacy. Romance, it turns out, has always found its architecture.

discovery_articles.title: Rare Fossil Reveals a Three-Tier Food Chain Frozen in Time: a Pterosaur Eaten by an Ichthyosaur Eaten by a Pliosaur
discovery_articles.snippet: Uncovered in part by amateur fossil hunters in Australia, the fossil preserves a unique look at prehistoric predatory dynamics
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A pterosaur inside an ichthyosaur inside a pliosaur — a Russian nesting doll of prehistoric predation, frozen mid-meal some 240 million years ago, and it took amateur fossil hunters to find it.

discovery_articles.title: Ice Age Humans Mostly Killed Female Woolly Mammoths, Suggests Ancient DNA
discovery_articles.snippet: After analyzing more than 500 mammoth bones, researchers found that ancient humans disproportionately hunted female mammoths for reasons still unknown
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Ancient hunters weren't just taking mammoths — they were disproportionately targeting females, a selective pressure that may have quietly accelerated a species toward extinction long before the last ice receded.

discovery_articles.title: Yellowstone Is Among the World's Best Places to See Wild Wolves. Here's the Story of the Animal Called Both 'Public Enemy' and Cultural Icon
discovery_articles.snippet: A century ago, resident wolves were eliminated from the park. In 1995, biologists brought them back, marking a historic reintroduction of a top carnivore
discovery_articles.ferns_note: When wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995, they didn't just restore a predator — they rewrote rivers, because elk stopped lingering near water, letting willows and aspens regrow and stabilize the banks. The ghost of a wolf is in the shape of a stream.

discovery_articles.title: This Man Turned Human Corpses Into Popular Museum Displays. Now, the Creator of These Controversial ‘Body Worlds’ Has Donated His Own Body to Science
discovery_articles.snippet: Gunther von Hagens, who invented plastination, a method of preserving bodies by replacing their natural fluids with polymers, recently died at age 81
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Gunther von Hagens spent his career turning death into spectacle for millions of museum visitors — and in the end, he handed his own body over to the very process he invented, the ultimate final commitment to his life's work.

discovery_articles.title: To detect CTE while alive, a test for another brain disease may help
discovery_articles.snippet: A protein that is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease may also ID a brain condition associated with head trauma in contact sports, early findings suggest.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A protein long associated with Alzheimer's may now offer the first real window into diagnosing CTE while a patient is still alive — which means the devastating brain damage seen in athletes might finally be something doctors can see before an autopsy.

discovery_articles.title: Heritage Bookbinding Elements Transform in Contemporary Sculptures by Adelene Koh
discovery_articles.snippet: For Koh, an under-appreciated element of a book's construction becomes the highlight. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Bookbinding's most invisible element — the structural sinew holding pages to spine — becomes the entire point in Adelene Koh's sculptures, a quiet argument that the parts we overlook are often the most worth examining.

featured_read.title: No One You Love Is Ever Dead: Hemingway on the Most Devastating of Losses and the Meaning of Life
featured_read.snippet: "We must live it, now, a day at a time and be very careful not to hurt each other."
featured_read.blurb: Hemingway, stripped of bravado, wrestles with whether grief is a form of continued love or simply its wreckage — and arrives somewhere unexpectedly tender. This one asks you to sit with the question of what we owe the living when we are still half-occupied by the dead.

garden_note.note: First light crept over the Zürichberg at 05:28 this morning, catching the late-summer dahlias mid-dew — August has arrived with that particular golden gravity that makes you want to be outside before breakfast. The tomatoes are swelling fast now and the basil is begging to be pinched before it bolts in the lingering warmth.
in_season: Dahlias — stake taller varieties before the August storms arrive
Tomatoes — check for ripening clusters daily and remove lower yellowing leaves
Basil — harvest generously to delay flowering
Courgettes — pick while small or find a marrow-sized surprise by evening
garden_note.sky_tonight: The waning gibbous moon rises late but blazes bright enough to cast shadows — look for Saturn low in the southeast as darkness settles.

news.title: Meera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for oyster mushroom burgers with five-spice cabbage | Meera Sodha recipes
news.snippet: These roasted oyster mushrooms are meaty, savoury and chewy, made even more satisfying in a south-east Asian-style dressing Not every plant makes a great burger filling. You might think pulses or potatoes for heft, but the lack of texture and propensity to mush can be unsatisfying. This is where mushrooms excel; they trade in satisfaction.
news.blurb: A timely reminder that the right mushroom, properly roasted and dressed with a little five-spice swagger, can outshine any beef patty at the table.

news.title: Where to Find the Best Cơm Tấm in Saigon
news.snippet: Alex Yem Born from broken rice grains once considered inferior, the city’s humble breakfast staple has become one of Vietnam’s most satisfying—and endlessly customizable—meals. The post Where to Find the Best Cơm Tấm in Saigon appeared first on Saveur .
news.blurb: A beautifully reported deep-dive into Saigon's beloved broken-rice dish — proof that the most satisfying meals are often born from humble, unlikely origins.

recipe.title: Cherry Jam
recipe.snippet: One of the first “recipes” on this blog was No-Recipe Cherry Jam, posted in 2005, which wasn’t quite a recipe. Nevertheless, a lot of people successfully used those guidelines to make cherry jam over the last fifteen years. The basis for it was how I’ve been making jam forever, using 3 parts sugar to 4 parts fruit puree.
recipe.blurb: David Lebovitz's proper Cherry Jam recipe is summer distilled into a jar — simple enough to make on a lazy afternoon and deeply rewarding every time you unscrew the lid in the darker months ahead.

larder.seasonal_note: Zürich's Tuesday and Saturday markets at Bürkliplatz are piled with Büezer tomatoes and golden Mirabellen right now — slice them together with a little fleur de sel and cold-pressed rapeseed oil for a breakfast that needs absolutely nothing else.

fern_data.greeting: Somewhere right now, a market vendor in Kawran Bazar is arranging the first wet bundles of herbs before the heat arrives — and this edition meets that same quiet industry with Diocletian rising from peasant obscurity to rescue an empire, a 17th-century queen being threaded into silk and fairy-tale, and liquid air batteries quietly rewriting what we thought energy storage could do.
